article_title: Considerations for Supporting a Successful Start to the 2020-2021 School Year for Students with Disabilities
citation: Considerations for supporting a successful start to the 2020-2021 school year for students with disabilities. (2020). National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), WestEd. https://ncsi.wested.org
title: Use Universal Design for Learning as the instructional foundation for all students in both distance and school-based settings
description: The guidance recommends that Universal Design for Learning (UDL) form the instructional foundation for all students as schools plan for in-person, distance, and blended service delivery. It states that "Universal Design for Learning (UDL) should form instructional foundation for all students" and that educators need support to ensure UDL is in place across settings. SEAs are asked how they are guiding general education teachers to understand and use UDL.
requirements: Educators need support to ensure UDL is in place in distance and school-based settings
target_learners: all students, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: access to standards-based instruction across in-person, distance, and blended delivery models
examples: The document pairs the premise with SEA guiding questions on how the agency is guiding general education teachers to understand and use UDL as a foundation for all instruction.
key_sources: Considerations for supporting a successful start to the 2020-2021 school year for students with disabilities. (2020). National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED609257

article_title: “AI is reducing options I had used”: exploring faculty perceptions of accessible course design in a ChatGPT world
citation: Gurher Sidhu, Fatima Atif, Franz Newland. (2025). "AI is reducing options I had used": exploring faculty perceptions of accessible course design in a ChatGPT world. York University. https://www.yorku.ca
title: Universal Design for Learning: three pillars of multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression
description: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is an inclusive pedagogy, inspired by universal design in architecture, that seeks to design learning environments accessible to as many learners as possible. Following its three pillars, "teachers should aim to provide: multiple means of engagement, or motivation, with course material; multiple means of representation... and, multiple means of action and expression, or diverse assessment methods". The study uses UDL as the framework against which faculty awareness and implementation of twenty techniques is assessed.
requirements: Sufficient uptake by professors for UDL to reduce the burden on accessibility services and students
constraints: UDL will not meet all students' needs and does not replace individual accommodations entirely
Applied in a post-secondary context where individual accommodations follow a medical model while UDL aligns with the social model of disability
target_learners: Post-secondary students, including those with and without formal accessibility needs
target_learning_goals: Accessible learning environments through multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression
examples: The survey rated faculty familiarity and implementation of twenty UDL techniques such as closed captioning, flexible deadlines, and OCR-readable PDFs
key_sources: Gurher Sidhu, Fatima Atif, Franz Newland. (2025). "AI is reducing options I had used": exploring faculty perceptions of accessible course design in a ChatGPT world. York University. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/e4hmv_v1

article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: Universal Design for Learning as a design lens grounded in learner variability
description: The statement grounds LUDIA in CAST's Universal Design for Learning framework, which supports educators in designing learning experiences and environments for the full range of learners, "anticipating and embracing variability from the start, rather than focusing on perceived deficits in learners". CAST states the premise as "there is no average brain. Variability is the dominant feature of the nervous system" and describes three principles — Engagement, Representation, and Action and Expression — as aligning to affective, recognition, and strategic networks, a framing CAST itself calls a simplified model useful for thinking about design rather than a claim about how the brain works. The Guidelines are a lens for finding barriers in existing designs, not a prescription or checklist, and Guidelines 3.0 positions UDL alongside asset-based approaches such as Funds of Knowledge and Disability Studies.
requirements: Educators or instructional designers must make the teaching-method decisions; the framework does not say which method to teach by
constraints: The authors note the evidence base of the framework LUDIA rests on is under active and legitimate challenge
UDL originated in the United States and its uptake in national policy is uneven
target_learners: Educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders designing for the full range of learners
target_learning_goals: Reducing barriers to learning while honouring learners' multiple identities and specific learning goals
key_sources: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en

article_title: Improving comprehension online: effects of deep vocabulary instruction with bilingual and monolingual fifth graders
citation: Proctor, C.P., Dalton, B., Uccelli, P., Biancarosa, G., Mo, E., Snow, C., & Neugebauer, S. (2011). Improving comprehension online: effects of deep vocabulary instruction with bilingual and monolingual fifth graders. Read Writ 24, 517–544. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9218-2
title: Internet-delivered universally designed multimedia vocabulary intervention with bilingual text access
description: An Internet-delivered intervention in which students read multimedia texts with embedded vocabulary instruction and reading strategy support, designed to be universally accessible to English-speaking and Spanish–English-speaking students. The article describes that "Intervention students read eight multimedia texts with embedded instruction on 40 words and reading strategy support" and that "Students could access all texts and activities in Spanish and English." It was evaluated against a control group over 16 weeks with 240 fifth graders.
requirements: Delivered via the Internet with multimedia texts and embedded instruction on targeted vocabulary words
constraints: Evaluated in a quasi-experimental design with fifth graders, about half Spanish–English bilinguals
examples: Intervention students read eight multimedia texts with embedded instruction on 40 words over a 16-week intervention, with all texts and activities accessible in Spanish and English.
key_sources: Proctor, C.P., Dalton, B., Uccelli, P., Biancarosa, G., Mo, E., Snow, C., & Neugebauer, S. (2011). Improving comprehension online: effects of deep vocabulary instruction with bilingual and monolingual fifth graders. Read Writ 24, 517–544. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9218-2

article_title: Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC)
citation: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4
title: Understanding Dementia MOOC (UDMOOC)
description: The UDMOOC is a free, 9-week online course from the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre aiming to improve dementia knowledge in a broad international community. It covers "basic neurobiology, dementia pathophysiology, medical management and person-centred care", and its "design includes a conversational framework, video discussions, summaries and transcripts, discussion forums, games and quizzes". It was designed to maximise accessibility for non-traditional adult learners who may have low levels of previous education.
requirements: Open enrolment with no exclusion criteria; content designed for accessibility for learners with low previous education
constraints: Completion requires participants to finish the final unit before the post-test survey to be counted in the evaluation
target_learning_goals: Understanding brain pathology associated with dementia and how it affects the person, to help carers comprehend and respond to behaviour
examples: Delivered free online in 2016 and 2017, enrolling 20,061 and 29,039 participants across 117 and 132 countries respectively
key_sources: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4

article_title: Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach
citation: Marvin Roski, Ratan Sebastian, Ralph Ewerth, Anett Hoppe, Andreas Nehring. (2024). Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach. Computers & Education 214 (2024) 105028. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105028
title: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) framework
description: UDL is a framework developed by CAST that aims to shape learning environments to be accessible and challenging for all learners, focusing on changing the environment rather than the learners. Its guidelines are structured according to three principles: "Provide multiple means of engagement", "Provide multiple means of representation", and "Provide multiple means of action and expression", operationalized through nine guidelines and 31 checkpoints with optional concrete suggestions such as audio and visual information, customizable interfaces, or glossaries.
requirements: Intentional design of the learning environment to minimize barriers; UDL suggestions are optional and require implementation decisions by designers
constraints: Experts' perceptions and interpretations of the guidelines vary due to the complexity of UDL, and the article notes implementations often lack sufficient detail, complicating the evidence base
target_learners: All learners in inclusive settings, including learners with disabilities or impairments
target_learning_goals: Accessible, meaningful and challenging learning experiences for all students; cultivating autonomous, self-responsible learners
examples: The I3Learn platform implements UDL checkpoints 1 (options for perception), 8.2 (vary demands and resources), and 9.3 (self-assessment and reflection), among others.
key_sources: Marvin Roski, Ratan Sebastian, Ralph Ewerth, Anett Hoppe, Andreas Nehring. (2024). Learning analytics and the Universal Design for Learning (UDL): A clustering approach. Computers & Education 214 (2024) 105028. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105028

article_title: Measuring the Effectiveness of Universal Design for Learning Intervention in Postsecondary Education
citation: Davies, P. L., Schelly, C. L., & Spooner, C. L. (2013). Measuring the Effectiveness of Universal Design for Learning Intervention in Postsecondary Education. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 26(3), 195-220. http://accessproject.colostate.edu/udl
title: Universal Design for Learning: three principles grounded in cognitive neuroscience
description: UDL is defined by the article as composed of three principles: "multiple means of representation", "multiple means of student action and expression", and "multiple means of student engagement". The framework holds that these principles map onto three groups of neural networks — recognition, strategic, and affective — whose interaction creates a model of cognition during learning episodes. The article distinguishes UDL from other universal design adaptations by its cognitive neuroscience foundation and its codification in federal law, and uses it as the training content and measurement frame for the intervention study.
requirements: Instructors need training on the three principles and techniques for implementing them in teaching and accessible course materials
constraints: UDL is distinguished from related adaptations (UDI, UID) by its neuroscience foundation and legal codification, as the article states
target_learners: postsecondary students, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: inclusive, equitable teaching and accessible course materials across psychology and higher education courses
examples: The research team trained nine intervention-section instructors on techniques and strategies addressing each of the three UDL principles during five weekly one-hour meetings
key_sources: Davies, P. L., Schelly, C. L., & Spooner, C. L. (2013). Measuring the Effectiveness of Universal Design for Learning Intervention in Postsecondary Education. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 26(3), 195-220. http://accessproject.colostate.edu/udl

article_title: Fostering interactive medical education: integrating Web 2.0 tools through a universal design for learning framework.
citation: E. Ergonul and S. Buyukcoban. (2026). Fostering interactive medical education: integrating Web 2.0 tools through a universal design for learning framework. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2639193
title: Universal Design for Learning as a three-principle framework for flexible, accessible learning design
description: The article uses the UDL model as the organising framework for its faculty development programme, describing it as "a systematic and evidence-based approach to designing learning materials, instructional methods, and assessment processes". UDL is structured around three principles — Engagement, Representation, and Action & Expression — each mapped in the study's design to a dominant brain region and to specific Web 2.0 tools (e.g. Wooclap and Padlet for Engagement; Thinglink, Mindmeister, Mindomo and Edpuzzle for Representation). The framework is intended to help students answer three questions: why, what, and how they are learning.
requirements: Technology integration aligned with UDL requires tools selected for accessibility, ease of use, interactivity, and alignment with UDL principles, as the article states guided its tool selection.
constraints: The article notes a significant gap in the literature regarding practical, evidence-based integration of UDL principles with Web 2.0 tools within medical education.
target_learning_goals: technology-enhanced teaching aligned to UDL principles
examples: Training sessions mapped each UDL principle to tools and activities, such as a KWL activity via Wooclap and Padlet for Engagement and concept mapping for a hypertension lesson for Representation.
key_sources: E. Ergonul and S. Buyukcoban. (2026). Fostering interactive medical education: integrating Web 2.0 tools through a universal design for learning framework. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2639193

article_title: Fostering interactive medical education: integrating Web 2.0 tools through a universal design for learning framework.
citation: E. Ergonul and S. Buyukcoban. (2026). Fostering interactive medical education: integrating Web 2.0 tools through a universal design for learning framework. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2639193
title: Two-year remote UDL-based faculty development programme with hands-on Web 2.0 tool training
description: A faculty development programme conducted remotely between 2020 and 2022 in which 262 medical faculty members were trained in UDL-aligned Web 2.0 tools (Padlet, Wooclap, Thinglink, Mindomo, Mindmeister, Edpuzzle, Google Forms, Formative, Kahoot). Each four-hour session was repeated 20 times over two years and delivered via the university's distance education platform. Overall satisfaction was moderately high (M = 3.90, SD = 1.1), with highest scores for pace of the training and likelihood of recommending it.
requirements: Sessions used the university's distance education platform and included interactive videos, collaborative group activities, and real-time Q&A sessions.
constraints: The programme's impact remained at an early stage: most educators did not use the tools after training, per the authors.
target_learners: medical faculty across basic, clinical, and surgical sciences departments
target_learning_goals: integrating Web 2.0 tools into flexible and interactive educational environments consistent with UDL principles
examples: Tools were selected based on their accessibility, ease of use, interactivity, and capacity to align with UDL principles.
key_sources: E. Ergonul and S. Buyukcoban. (2026). Fostering interactive medical education: integrating Web 2.0 tools through a universal design for learning framework. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2639193

article_title: Assessment IS learning: developing a student-centred approach for assessment in Higher Education.
citation: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921
title: Design assessments inclusively using Universal Design for Learning principles and student choice
description: Assessments should be inclusive and equitable for all learners, including students with disabilities, neurodiversities, different cultures, or studying in a non-native language. The article states that 'Engaging with concepts promoting equity in assessment, such as Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles can be a major assistance in ensuring inclusive practice', listing three principles adapted to assessment: engagement (optionality welcoming different identities and capacities), representation (relatable language, examples and symbols), and actions and expression (optionality in assessment type, timing, focus or length). Choice of subject matter or assessment mode benefits all learners, not only those with specific needs.
requirements: Where essential performative skills or competencies must be evaluated, support needs to be provided to students with additional needs; marking criteria can remain consistent across modes with criteria set separately for each delivery mode
constraints: The article notes the term authentic assessment is considered controversial or pejorative by some; Tai et al. argue all aspects of assessment—subject matter, modality, purpose, timing, procedures—need rethinking to build in accommodations
target_learners: students with disabilities or neurodiversities, students studying in a non-native language, and diverse student groups in higher education
target_learning_goals: equal opportunity to perform to the fullest in assessment
examples: The review suggests building in options such as choosing a written output or a presentation, so students with disabilities of the written word have a viable alternative while those with anxiety or confidence challenges are also accommodated
key_sources: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921

article_title: Teachers' involvement and students' self-efficacy: Keys to achievement in higher education.
citation: Ayllón Sara, Alsina Ángel, Colomer Jordi. (2019). Teachers’ involvement and students’ self-efficacy: Keys to achievement in higher education. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0216865
title: University of Girona teaching-evaluation dataset (86,038 student records, 2014–2016) with released microdata and Stata code
description: The study's empirical base is the universe of anonymous on-line teaching evaluations collected via Moodle three weeks before final exams at the University of Girona over three years. It comprises "86,038 complete students' records", information on 2,204 different course subjects and 1,832 evaluated teachers, with achievement (final marks 0–10, mean 6.98) linked from student records. The microdata and the Stata econometric code are openly available via the Dryad repository link the article prints.
requirements: Access depends on the anonymised microdata deposited at the printed Dryad DOI (10.5061/dryad.601k960)
constraints: Questionnaire completion was voluntary, so the authors state they do not know whether the sample represents all students at the university
examples: Questionnaire answers on a 1–5 scale with means around 4; achievement mean of 6.98 (SD 1.52)
key_sources: Ayllón Sara, Alsina Ángel, Colomer Jordi. (2019). Teachers’ involvement and students’ self-efficacy: Keys to achievement in higher education. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0216865
